item.title: Intrinsic volume fraction can decouple from hydrodynamic size in p(NIPAm-co-AA) microgels
item.description: arXiv:2611.28284v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantifying the packing fraction of microgels is key to understanding their rheology and transport properties. Often, packing fractions are extrapolated from the hydrodynamic size and intrinsic volume fraction under the assumption that particle size and polymer volume change are proportional. Here, we test this assumption for p(N-isopropylacrylamide-co-acrylic acid) [p(NIPAm-co-AA)] microgels of two crosslinker concentrations (1 wt\% and 7 wt\% methylenebisacrylamide) using capillary viscometry and light scattering (static and dynamic) above and below the pKa of acrylic acid (AA). At pH 8, where AA is fully ionized, the microgels do not undergo a pronounced volume phase transition because electrostatic repulsion hinders thermal collapse, and both measures of hydrodynamic volume are equal. At pH 4, however, p(NIPAm-co-AA) microgels are weakly charged and exhibit a volume phase transition near the lower critical solution temperature of pNIPAm; the magnitude of the size change is greater for the less-crosslinked microgel. Above the volume phase transition temperature, the volume change from hydrodynamic radius decouples from that from viscosity. The ratio of the radius of gyration and hydrodynamic radius R_g/R_h of p(NIPAm-co-AA) microgels at high temperature exceeds the value theoretically predicted for homogeneous spheres and the deviation increases with the extent of crosslinking, suggesting that a non-uniform internal distribution of polymer gives rise to the anomalous decoupling at high temperatures. Our results indicate that care must be taken in extrapolating packing fractions for multi-responsive copolymer microgels, and suggest that copolymer composition and crosslink density may be used to tune bulk properties such as rheology through the internal microstructure.
item.dc:creator: Peter Edimeh, Howard Chen, Jacinta C. Conrad

item.title: Exploring new speciation patterns: architecture of genetic similarity networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.28358v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We use an individual based model to identify signatures of speciation modes in genetic similarity networks. These networks group individuals based on their genetic similarity, defined through Hamming distances between binary strings representing their genomes. The results of our extensive simulations demonstrate that sympatric and parapatric speciation modes are clearly distinguishable and measurable through specific network metrics. In particular, structural properties -- including clustering coefficient, mean degree, geodesic distance, and assortativity -- show significant differences in both stationary values and transient phases, giving rise to a novel framework for distinguishing between speciation modes.
item.dc:creator: David M. Schneider, Claudio Pastorino

item.title: Geometry Reorganizes Nonequilibrium States that Gate Topological Switching in an Active Polymer
item.description: arXiv:2611.29649v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Even under identical external conditions, a driven system can occupy distinct long-lived states with different susceptibilities to the same rare transition. We demonstrate this in a confined partially active polymer, where independent unknotted replicas occupy distinct mechanical states with different topological futures. Matched-control and event-resolved analyses reveal a susceptible reservoir and a short threading precursor. We test this state dependence prospectively by launching 2272 Langevin-noise branches from 71 preserved unknotted phase-space states using a classifier prespecified from independent data. Most strikingly, the same classifier strongly separates finite-time knotting at one pore radius, yet reverses its susceptibility ordering at a neighboring radius. Thus geometry does not merely shift an average knotting rate; it selects among long-lived nonequilibrium states and reorganizes the mapping between a pre-existing mechanical coordinate and future topological fate.
item.dc:creator: Shiqi Zhou

item.title: Elastic crumple pair potentials
item.description: arXiv:2611.29654v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Thin structures across scales and materials, from graphene sheets to clothing to aircraft skins, respond to forcing and confinement by crumpling, with deformation localized into zones of characteristic shape. Much attention has been paid to isolated crescent vertex and ridge shapes, but there has been almost no investigation into the dynamics, creation/destruction, and interactions between multiple vertices (``crumples'') that are inherent in nearly all deformation processes. The next step beyond single crumples are pair interactions, mediated by background curvature. Of these, we focus on two common types, using a quasi-1D setup allowing controlled boundary motion and force measurement coupled with tracking of crumple positions. We provide experimental evidence for non-monotonic pair potentials, with short-range attraction, long-range repulsion, and an intermediate forbidden region. We construct a phenomenological energy that reproduces the bifurcations and the interrelations between observed quantities. These results provide a new insight and input towards understanding and building reduced descriptions of dynamic deformation and pattern formation and evolution in thin elastic plate and shell structures.
item.dc:creator: D. Gimeno, E. Hamm, J. A. Hanna

item.title: Principles of Material Memory
item.description: arXiv:2611.29774v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Materials keep traces of how they were driven: a field leaves a magnetization behind, and a sequence of forces can leave a pattern that records the order in which they acted. It remains open what such a history records, which interactions create the record and which dynamics preserve it. This review relates the three. Forces applied in different orders can leave different states after the drive is removed, and in a spatial network the preferred local arrangements may not be reconcilable around a closed loop. Both effects compare two paths, one in time and one around a loop in space, and both are described by commutators, curvature and holonomy. Restoring forces and fluctuations then set how long the trace survives: a displacement relaxes, a phase diffuses, and barriers protect a pattern against rare thermal transitions. Near an instability, a weak writing bias is amplified while the coordinate that carries the state has no restoring force, and the barriers that retain the chosen state form only afterwards. The choice is therefore as accurate as the detection of the bias against the noise during the time for which the coordinate is free. Once a state is stored behind a barrier, a static bias replaces it through the same thermal channel by which it would be lost. The ratio of the mean retention time to the mean rewriting time is then bounded, up to a prefactor close to one, by the Boltzmann factor of an effective energy bias, whatever the height of the barrier. Calculations for capillary rotors and point-dipole arrays show how the geometry of the interactions constrains the patterns that a material can store. In a model of three coupled amplitudes, a weak bias makes two mirror-image patterns lose stability at slightly different coupling strengths, so that a coupling pulse between the two thresholds erases one pattern and preserves the other.
item.dc:creator: Vladimir A. Baulin

item.title: Solids activated by multi-body nonreciprocity
item.description: arXiv:2611.30058v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Field-mediated forces between particles can be both nonreciprocal and irreducibly multi-body, giving rise to emergent activity in systems of individually passive particles. While prior work extensively studied how multi-body nonreciprocity can activate few-body systems, fuel intermittency, and drive liquid-like behavior, the effect on the solid state of large particle ensembles is less explored. Here we use two-dimensional, close-packed rafts of identical, athermal, acoustically levitated microspheres to show how multi-body nonreciprocity injects activity in solids. At the level of both individual particles and collective dynamics, crystalline rafts exhibit persistent circulations with no net handedness. The rafts also exhibit a phonon-like dispersion relation corresponding to a large Poisson ratio, indicating an induced softness to shear. Within the bulk, lattice symmetry masks microscopic nonreciprocity, although it can manifest in renormalized, reciprocal elastic coefficients. At dislocations and raft edges, where this symmetry is broken, multi-body nonreciprocal interactions act as local generators of activity. A coarse-grained microscopic model of multi-body nonreciprocity, calibrated on three-particle simulations, recovers the rafts' experimentally observed dispersion relations and localized activity. Using these findings, we illustrate how to harness defect-induced activity for programmable movement by arranging microscopic dislocations to drive macroscopic propulsion and rotation of a whole raft.
item.dc:creator: Brady Wu, Daniel S. Seara, Qinghao Mao, Vincenzo Vitelli, Heinrich M. Jaeger

item.title: Dynamical evolution and rheological behavior of a sheared compound vesicle with a highly viscous core: a mesoscale particle-based study
item.description: arXiv:2611.30232v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study numerically the dynamics and the rheology of a two-dimensional compound vesicle in wall-bounded shear flow, as a minimal model of a nucleated cell. We consider the configuration in which the annular fluid is iso-viscous with the external one, while the inner core is more viscous. Increasing the core viscosity drives the external vesicle away from steady tank-treading at values $\phi \geq 0.6$. When an internal body is present, the annular fluid partially shields the outer membrane from the viscous core, so that at small filling fractions the external vesicle retains tank-treading with a higher inclination angle and the intrinsic viscosity stays comparatively low. The internal vesicle, by contrast, tumbles and migrates away from the center, and at high $\phi$ this motion couples back to the host, producing intermittent shape excursions of the external membrane. The inner viscous body thus acts as an internal governor of the dynamical state.
item.dc:creator: A. Lamura

item.title: Growing Knot Embeddings into Spherical Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2611.30245v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Knotted structures occur throughout soft matter and biology, where topological constraints can shape relaxation and spatial organization. Here, we introduce a computational construction that maps a specific 3D knot embedding to a graph embedded on the sphere through growth and interfacial-energy relaxation. For standard 3D embeddings of prime knots with at most seven crossings, we obtain a family of growth-based graphs that generally differ from the corresponding Tait graphs. We further identify an empirical growth-graph reconstruction rule based on polygonal regions with alternating crossing structure in a knot diagram. Non-minimal diagrams demonstrate that these graphs are not knot invariants, while selected connected sums suggest that graph features associated with their prime factors can remain recognizable. Determining how these graphs transform under isotopy may reveal invariant features, which we leave for future study.
item.dc:creator: Eren G\"ulmez, Joost de Graaf

item.title: Dynamics of the Nuclear Envelope and Mitotic Spindle in Closed Mitosis
item.description: arXiv:2611.28302v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: During closed mitosis, large-scale deformation of the nuclear envelope is driven by the mitotic spindle and chromosomes contained within it. Previous models of closed mitosis have established that the spatial distribution of spindle-generated forces influences nuclear morphology, but have imposed axisymmetry and focused on equilibrium shapes. We introduce a three-dimensional biophysical model of nuclear envelope remodeling and spindle elongation that incorporates thermal fluctuations to examine how spindle-generated forces, chromatin distribution, and nuclear envelope elasticity control nuclear shape in fission yeast. The model reproduces features of both successful and aberrant nuclear shape change, including centering of mispositioned spindles, the dumbbell nuclear shape transition, and the formation of nuclear protrusions. A phase diagram of nuclear shape shows that insufficient spindle force produces elongated but undivided nuclei, while sufficiently large spindle forces produce either symmetric division or envelope tethers, depending on the size of the chromatin-envelope contact region. Near the boundary between symmetric division and tethering, nuclei develop asymmetric single-tether configurations. A reduced-order representation of the coupled envelope-spindle system shows a symmetry-breaking transition between symmetric and asymmetric nuclear shapes. Below a critical chromatin-envelope contact size, symmetric configurations lose stability during spindle elongation and thermal fluctuations drive nuclear shape trajectories toward one of two stable asymmetric configurations. These findings identify a growth-driven mechanical mechanism for spindle centering and alignment during early mitosis and reveal how asymmetric nuclear morphologies can arise during anaphase even in the absence of structural differences between the two spindle poles.
item.dc:creator: Wilson Lough, Zachary R. Gergely, Eduardo Corona, Meredith D. Betterton

item.title: Distinguishing photothermal and photoelectrokinetic contributions to flow in light-activated microchannel architectures
item.description: arXiv:2611.28481v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Light-driven flows near Janus surfaces could power microfluidic devices without external hardware. These flows are often attributed to photoinduced electro- or diffusio-osmosis, but illumination also heats the surface, potentially driving natural convection. Here, we map flow and temperature around a UVA-illuminated TiO$_2$-Au Janus membrane using depth-resolved particle tracking and infrared thermometry. Recirculating rolls form on both sides, with no measurable net flow across the membrane. Their cubic, reversing velocity profile identifies horizontal (Hadley) convection, driven by a lateral temperature gradient as the gold film absorbs light. The measured profile agrees with wall-corrected Hadley theory using one fitted parameter. Adding 100 mM NaCl to suppress electrokinetic flows leaves the profile unchanged, indicating that convection dominates. Simulations show that convection falls below 1 $\mu$m/s in thin channels, where surface-driven osmotic flows could dominate. Thus, device geometry and surface chemistry determine which mechanism governs light-driven microfluidic flows.
item.dc:creator: Sudharshan Anandan, Yuhang Fang, Lily Farmer, Maria Irineu, Shanmukhi Sripada, Tyler Hughes, Jared Nathan, Sathish Rajendran, Steven Wereley, Amy Marconnet, Thomas Beechem, Jeffrey L. Moran, David M. Warsinger

item.title: An informational interpretation of the reverse nonequilibrium molecular dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2611.29174v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reverse nonequilibrium molecular dynamics (RNEMD) is an efficient simulation method for determining transport coefficients. In this method, a flux is imposed by a seemingly artificial nonlocal exchange operation and the corresponding thermodynamic gradient is induced as a result, apparently reversing the usual force-flux causality. Although this method is well studied as a simulation technique, developing an information-thermodynamic interpretation of its Maxwell-demon-type operation and the associated apparent reversal of force-flux causality would provide a solid physical foundation for algorithms of this type. Here, we develop an information-reservoir interpretation for a representative RNEMD scheme for determining self-diffusivity. We show that the statistical bias of the information reservoir defines an information affinity that sustains a concentration gradient and a diffusive flux in the steady state. We further derive the linear transport coefficient corresponding to the information affinity in the linear response regime. Using the large deviation functional for the steady-state densities and currents, we also establish a fluctuation theorem for entropy production and the thermodynamic uncertainty relation linking entropy production to the fluctuations of the particle current. Computer simulations are performed to corroborate our theoretical results.
item.dc:creator: Yuxing Jiao, Mingcheng Yang

item.title: Dynamic Renewal for Hydrodynamic Coupling in Ciliary Mucus Transport
item.description: arXiv:2611.29378v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Mucociliary clearance in large mammalian airways involves millimetric MUC5B-rich mucus strands that emerge from submucosal glands approximately aligned with the direction of transport. These strands are observed downstream in cross-flow networks. Recently, Bos et al. [PNAS Nexus 2, pgad388 (2023)] modeled single strand reorientation using a free-draining coupling for the flow induced by cilia. This leaves unresolved whether the strand's own disturbance of the surrounding liquid assists or frustrates the turning. Here, we develop the methodology to address this question. An immersed-boundary coupling is combined with a Fourier-space Stokes solver and a bespoke dynamic-renewal algorithm that exposes the strand to new ciliary domain without enlarging the simulation volume. This allows us to overcome one of the multiscale challenges posed by mucociliary clearance. We find that hydrodynamic interactions result in only a limited decrease in the rate of reorientation, which supports the use of the free-draining approximation. Future work can build on the methodological foundation introduced here to study collective strand dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Jeroen Bechtold, Valentijn van Zwieten, Iris Verkuil, Meike F. Bos, Georg Rempfer, Mae Nesenberend, Pieter Michels, Florian K. R. Gaeremynck, Bart Stam, Debabrata Panja, Joost de Graaf

item.title: Exact superdiffusion exponents and hull exploration of chiral random walkers on critical percolation clusters
item.description: arXiv:2611.29537v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generalizing de Gennes' ant-in-the-labyrinth concept, we consider a chiral random walker on a percolation cluster at criticality. The fully chiral ant clings to obstacle boundaries and traces the fractal hulls of the cluster, spreading with the exact walk dimension $7/4$ until its orbit closes. Because the cluster contains holes on all scales, the ensemble spreads superdiffusively, $\langle r^2\rangle\sim t^{89/84}$, carried by a diminishing fraction of walkers whose orbits are still open. Both exponents follow from percolation geometry alone, and agree well with large-scale numerical simulations. When the walker turns chirally only with probability $\chi<1$, superdiffusion gives way to the subdiffusion of the ant at a crossover time set by both exponents, with a diffusion coefficient enhanced by $(1-\chi)^{-2/d_w}$. The relation between crossover time and diffusion coefficient does not depend on how chirality is realized, offering a direct test for chiral tracers in disordered media.
item.dc:creator: Joshua Uhlig, Ralf Metzler, Erik Kalz

item.title: Geometric Polarization-Virial Theorems for Field-Induced Dipolar Interactions and Force Reversal
item.description: arXiv:2611.30039v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Electric fields can turn attraction into repulsion between far-separated atoms, yet the complete angular mechanical structure governing this reversal has remained unknown. Here, we uncover an entropy-like geometric structure: the cubically weighted interaction free energy, r^3 F(r), is nondecreasing under physical dilation. This structure unifies two exact polarization-virial theorems for arbitrary stable quasistatic dipole assemblies and fully retarded dipole pairs under stated conditions. Consequently, the free energy has at most one zero and energetic cancellation precedes mechanical cancellation. A force zero retains strictly positive energy, whereas an energy zero retains an attractive force. The resulting analytical angular fine structure is resolved by a quantum harmonic oscillator pair, yielding the complete arbitrary-angle interaction energy and radial force that recover quantum-perturbative results. The conventional dipolar magic angle splits into strictly ordered energy- and force-zero angles; the latter uniquely bounds the radially repulsive sector and carries a positive energy barrier. Derived scaling laws and finite-sphere calculations provide experimentally testable signatures from microscopic dipoles to macroscopic polarizable bodies.
item.dc:creator: Shuze Zhu

item.title: Impact of Topology and Sequence Length on the Pressure-Dependent Collapsibility of Proteins
item.description: arXiv:2611.30336v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Several physical and evolutionary factors, including temperature, pressure, solvent quality, and natural selection, influence how amino acid sequences adopt their native structures. Although protein folding has been extensively studied, the physical determinants of protein collapse and their relationship to native-state folding remain less understood. In particular, "collapsibility", the intrinsic propensity of a protein sequence to form compact conformations, is distinct from but closely related to "foldability", the ability to reach the native structure. Previous theoretical studies suggested that collapsibility is encoded in native-state topology, potentially reflecting evolutionary selection. However, the roles of solvent-mediated interactions and hydrostatic pressure remain unclear. Here, we extend the theoretical framework of protein collapsibility by incorporating a pressure-dependent desolvation potential to investigate how hydrostatic pressure influences protein collapse. We find that increasing pressure destabilizes the fully folded native state, but can still favor the compact, water-mediated conformations. Furthermore, the magnitude and direction of pressure-induced changes in collapsibility depend strongly on native-state topology, including secondary and tertiary structures. Proteins and domains with a higher proportion of non-local native contacts generally exhibit greater pressure-induced water-mediated collapsibility. These findings highlight the role of native-state topology in determining the pressure sensitivity of protein collapse and provide insights into the interplay among protein structure, solvent-mediated interactions, and environmental perturbations.
item.dc:creator: Jiayi Wang, D. Thirumalai, Margaret S. Cheung, Andrei G. Gasic

item.title: Nonequilibrium Dynamics of R-loop Formation in the CRISPR-Cas9 System
item.description: arXiv:2611.30527v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The binding specificity of CRISPR-Cas9 is governed by the stepwise formation of an R-loop, in which the sgRNA displaces the nontarget DNA strand and hybridizes with the target strand in discrete base pair steps. Here we develop a nonequilibrium dynamics framework that models R-loop formation as a continuous-time Markov birth-death process over twenty base pairs. Each transition rate is derived from Eyring transition-state theory and the Bell model, and combines three physical contributions, i.e., the torsional strain generated by the B-form to A-form helical conversion at the unwinding front, a base stacking correction that couples neighboring base pairs, and the allosteric work supplied by Cas9 conformational changes. We further derive the entropy production of the process, which is decomposed into activation, stacking, torsional, and allosteric terms. The resulting prediction model uses no external thermodynamic database and reaches Spearman correlations of 0.84 and 0.82 in two independent libraries of dCas9-sgRNA mismatch variants measured in vivo. The mismatch-type dependence is carried by one twist deviation and one pairing weight per type. Our model recovers the seed region sensitivity, the PAM-proximal activity gradient, and the moderate cost of dDrG mismatches, while isolating the high-activity double mismatch tail as the regime in which the present free-energy mapping is inadequate. The framework gives quantitative predictions on how DNA supercoiling and sequence context modulate binding affinity, and provides a mechanistic basis for sgRNA design.
item.dc:creator: Yu Liu, Bing Miao

item.title: Statistical mechanics of noisy collisions in active matter: Dyson-Landau theory
item.description: arXiv:2611.30910v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Active systems and other coarse-grained descriptions are often modeled by generalized dynamics, effective equations of motion that are not bound by the constraints of genuinely microscopic physics. In particular, these equations are generally stochastic on the smallest resolved scale. This poses a challenge to first-principles statistical physics, which usually derives emergent noise on larger scales from deterministic interactions. Here, we show how to systematically incorporate microscopic noise into kinetic theory in the limit of weak noise, i.e., high activity. By means of a Dyson expansion of the noisy free propagator, we derive the leading correction to the Landau kinetic equation for weakly interacting systems. We find that the common practice of combining a deterministic collision integral with the diffusive terms of the Fokker--Planck equation is the correct leading order. For dry aligning active matter, however, the corrections are non-analytic in the noise strength, as nearly parallel particles interact for arbitrarily long times. For noise that acts only during interactions, a minimal model of stochastic interactions, noise and collisions do not decouple: the leading corrections are odd in the coupling strength, partly logarithmically enhanced, and amount to an orientation-dependent effective noise strength. Agent-based simulations confirm the predicted dependence on the sign of the coupling. Even in this minimal model, the effect of noise on collisions can thus not be inferred from symmetry alone.
item.dc:creator: Horst-Holger Boltz, Max-Robin Schultz, Thomas Ihle

item.title: Donnan Grand Canonical Monte Carlo Simulations with Fast Ewald Summation for Calculating Individual Ionic Chemical Potentials
item.description: arXiv:2611.30961v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present a Donnan Grand Canonical Monte Carlo (GCMC) simulation method using fast Ewald summation to accurately and efficiently calculate the individual ionic excess chemical potentials of $\alpha_+:\alpha_-$ electrolyte solutions. By introducing a dynamic inner electrostatic potential that acts to penalize net charge fluctuations and maintain average charge neutrality ($\langle Q_t \rangle = 0$), the method enables single-ion GCMC trial moves without sacrificing convergence speed or breaking thermodynamic consistency. Unlike the Widom particle insertion method---which suffers from severe phase-space sampling bottlenecks and requires separate virtual insertions for each ionic species---the Donnan GCMC protocol simultaneously yields the individual excess chemical potentials $\mu_+^{\text{ex}}$ and $\mu_-^{\text{ex}}$ corresponding to a resulting bulk concentration $c_b$ with rapid numerical convergence. Varying the reference activity parameter $c_r$ allows us to efficiently construct the complete $\mu_\pm^{\text{ex}}(c_b)$ curves. Comparison with the Mean Spherical Approximation (MSA) demonstrates excellent agreement for size-symmetric electrolytes, while highlighting the failure of linear-response theories for size-asymmetric ions where electrostatic correlations and cavity effects become strongly coupled.
item.dc:creator: Alexandre P. dos Santos, Amin Bakhshandeh, Yan Levin

item.title: Phase separation by polar active transport
item.description: arXiv:2604.01057v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose an active Cahn-Hilliard theory for the dynamics of a new type of phase transition where the driving force is not the direct interactions between the two separating components, but their active sorting by a third polar species. This third species can transport the other two along its polarity in opposite directions, thus separating them. Inspired by recent experiments where molecular motors that walk in opposite directions along microtubules are sorted into separated domains, our theoretical description of this process introduces a new mechanism for active phase separation and could serve as a model for the organization of biological material in space inside cells. We predict the formation of motor domains, and further show that they can either coarsen to form macroscopic phases or reach a finite micro- or mesoscopic steady state size, these latter due to an arrest of coarsening through activity.
item.dc:creator: Sudipta Pattanayak, Alfredo Sciortino, Laurent Blanchoin, Manuel Th\'ery, Jean-Francois Joanny

item.title: Universal swelling of tangentially driven ring polymers in two dimensions
item.description: arXiv:2607.09436v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The interplay of tangential activity and excluded-volume interactions in ring polymers adsorbed to a surface, consistently results in the overall swelling of the ring configurations. This is in strong contrast to the case for three dimensional linear and ring polymers, where activity induces frequently collapsed structures. By means of Brownian Dynamic simulations, we investigate how the scaling properties of such active rings can be universally characterized by an activity-dependent Flory exponent, as a generalization of the equilibrium behavior. At high activity, an effective persistence length characterizes the conformations of active flexible rings.
item.dc:creator: Antonio Lamura, Marisol Ripoll

item.title: Microscopically informed constitutive framework for stress overshoot, yielding, and strain hardening in amorphous materials
item.description: arXiv:2607.13734v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop a microscopic constitutive theory for the nonlinear deformation of metallic and polymer glasses based on nonaffine elasticity coupled to irreversible many-body relaxation. The theory predicts the full stress--strain response, from linear elasticity through stress overshoot and yielding to steady plastic flow. We show that stress overshoot originates from the competition between a nonaffine elastic instability induced by strain-driven loss of mechanical connectivity at the atomic/molecular level, and viscous dissipation associated with structural relaxation. For polymer glasses, finite chain extensibility naturally accounts for strain hardening at large deformation. The stretched-exponential relaxation exponent is obtained independently from stress or modulus relaxation measurements and provides the primary dynamical input to the theory. Using a small set of physically meaningful parameters, the model quantitatively reproduces experimental stress--strain curves for metallic glasses, polycarbonate, PMMA, and epoxy resins over a broad range of strain rates. These results establish a unified microscopic framework linking relaxation dynamics, yielding, plastic flow, and strain hardening in amorphous solids.
item.dc:creator: Ankit Singh, Valeriy V. Ginzburg, Alessio Zaccone

item.title: Random close packing at extreme size ratios with an Adam-based inflation protocol
item.description: arXiv:2608.12235v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present \texttt{rcpgenerator}, an openly available code for generating $d$-dimensional dense, disordered, non-overlapping close packings from an arbitrary prescribed list of particle diameters. The method adapts the Clarke--Wiley inflation protocol, but instead uses the Adam optimizer to relax the particle configuration. Typically, particle coordinates are advanced with a single, global step size, which must shrink as the size ratio $S\equiv D_{\max}/D_{\min}$ grows, generally stalling the optimization. Adam instead gives each coordinate its own adaptive step size, stabilizing the optimization time across a broader range of $S$. We demonstrate this in three-dimensional periodic tests that reach $S\sim5\times10^{5}$ for a continuous lognormal distribution ($N\sim10^{6}$ diameters) and particle numbers up to $N\approx5.6\times10^{6}$ for power-law distributions, with the densest packings reaching $\phi\simeq0.87$, each completed in minutes to hours on a multicore machine. Across truncated-lognormal, truncated-power-law, and Weibull distributions, the resulting $\phi$ reproduces trends such as the locations of peaks and knees with distribution shape and $S$ found in prior numerical results and in the parameter-free Farr--Groot prediction, with a remaining offset typically $0.005$--$0.01$. Additionally, results are commensurate with multimodal packing densities measured in vibrated-bed experiments. The code and the complete per-case census behind every figure are released with the paper.
item.dc:creator: Kenneth W. Desmond

item.title: Liquid-liquid phase transitions in dipolar liquids. Insights into Supercooled Water
item.description: arXiv:2609.02666v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Dipolar liquids combine two coupled degrees of freedom, translational and dipolar. Intriguingly, these two sectors can reside in distinct thermodynamic states, with the state of one sector possibly favouring a specific state of the other. The onset of ferroelectric order in dipolar liquids is an example of this mutual stabilization. Since this coupling is often encoded in interaction potentials, projecting out one sector to derive an effective interaction for the other can uncover the microscopic mechanism underlying this phenomenon. A coarse-grained theory, solved in the large-dimensional limit, in which the distance between nearest-neighbour particles depends on their dipolar interaction through a density-dependent mechanical compliance shows that a ferroelectric transition can trigger a liquid-liquid transition. It also predicts a first-order liquid-liquid transition within the paraelectric phase that, in turn, can promote ferroelectric ordering. The anisotropic dipolar-dependent soft-core interaction is shown to lead to an effective Jagla-like isotropic two-length-scale interaction, known to support liquid-liquid phase transitions. Here, however, the two-length-scale pattern depends on density and dipolar configuration, and is therefore sensitive to dipolar order. Analysis of supercooled TIP4P/Ice water molecular dynamics simulations shows that first-coordination-shell features of the pair correlation functions are sensitive to dipolar interaction, supporting the foundations of the coarse-grained theory. Comparison of low- and high-density liquid water reveals enhanced spatial anisotropy of the first coordination shell in the low-density liquid, associated, within the theory, with increased effective excluded volume, showing that the liquid-liquid transition involves structural changes within the first shell, beyond reorganization of the interstitial region and tetrahedral order.
item.dc:creator: Maria Grazia Izzo

item.title: Composition-dependent nonlinear viscoelastic-viscoplastic behavior and constitutive framework for digitally mixed polymers spanning the glass transition
item.description: arXiv:2609.04399v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multi-material PolyJet printing produces voxel-scale digital mixtures of an elastomeric photopolymer (Agilus) and a glassy photopolymer (Vero), giving a material family whose room-temperature response ranges from elastomeric to glassy. Large-deformation uniaxial compression over nearly three orders of magnitude in strain rate reveals a nonlinear, rate-dependent load-unload response that evolves continuously with composition, from recoverable elastomeric hysteresis to glassy yield with post-yield softening, hardening, and substantial residual strain. Dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) shows that each mixture has a single glass transition temperature ($T_g$) that shifts to higher temperature with both Vero fraction and frequency, so composition acts much as temperature or loading rate does. This time-composition equivalence motivates one constitutive structure for the whole family: an equilibrium hyperelastic network with three non-equilibrium, rate-dependent branches carrying reptational, intermolecular, and glassy resistance. Its properties are anchored at the two endpoints and interpolated by smooth composition scaling laws. The model captures the compression response of all seven calibrated compositions and predicts a withheld mixture from the scaling laws alone, as well as the plane-strain compression and uniaxial tension responses of three representative compositions. Resolving the predicted stress into its branches shows the load passing from the elastomeric to the glassy mechanism, and the work from elastic storage to dissipation, as Vero content and rate rise. The glass transition that DMA maps at small strain therefore governs the large-strain deformation mechanisms. The framework gives a compact, physically based description of digitally mixed polymers and a predictive basis for designing functionally graded, architected multi-material structures.
item.dc:creator: Beijun Shen, Mary C. Boyce

item.title: Self organisation of invasive breast cancer driven by the interplay of active and passive nematic dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2412.01285v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In invasive breast cancer, cell clusters of varying sizes and shapes are embedded in the fibrous extracellular matrix (ECM). Although the prevailing view attributes this structure to increasing disorder resulting from loss of function and dedifferentiation, our findings reveal that it arises through a process of active self-organization driven by cancer cell motility. Simulations and histological analyses of tumours from over 2,000 breast cancer patients reveal that motile, aligned cancer cells within clusters move as active nematic aggregates through the surrounding highly aligned ECM fibres, which form a confining, passive nematic phase. Cellular motion leads to cluster splitting and coalescence. The degree of cluster activity, combined with heterogeneity in cell motility, is reflected in specific scaling behaviours for cluster shape, size distribution, and the distance between cluster boundaries and nematic defects in ECM alignment. Increased activity estimates correlate with tumour progression and are associated with a poorer prognosis for patients.

item.title: A Polarization Hall Effect in Hydrated DNA
item.description: arXiv:2601.06089v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We report magnetic-field- and temperature-dependent transverse-voltage phenomena in hydrated genomic DNA. The sample is confined beneath a glass coverslip in a quasi-two-dimensional geometry and subjected to perpendicular magnetic fields, revealing sharp thresholds, staircase-like voltage plateaus, and oscillatory structures approximately periodic in inverse magnetic field. Fixed-field cooling reveals longitudinal reorganizations near 20.6 and 12.0 $^\circ$C, while a separate experiment shows large-amplitude transverse oscillations below approximately 12 $^\circ$C. Water controls and buffer-free DNA measurements support an association between the structured response and the hydrated DNA system. We propose a polarization-based interpretation of the transverse response, termed a ``polarization Hall effect,'' and discuss the observed regimes within a phenomenological framework of nonlinear dynamics and metastable configurations. These findings identify hydrated DNA as a soft-matter system exhibiting structured electrical responses jointly regulated by magnetic field and temperature.

item.title: Uniaxial poroelastic tendon model with crimped fibre recruitment reveals hysteresis
item.description: arXiv:2606.24393v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Fibre recruitment plays an important role in tendon. Due to their large water content, a popular modelling approach for tendons is poroelasticity. Within this framework some tendon studies have included fibres, though none have included crimped fibre recruitment. We present a one dimensional poroelastic model in which the solid skeleton is composed of a soft neo-Hookean background matrix and crimped fibrils which do not bear load (FIB model). As the tissue is stretched, fibrils are straightened and contribute to load bearing. The fibre-reinforced tissue is compared to a tissue with a purely neo-Hookean (NH) skeleton in response to a uniaxial constant applied load (loading) and release of the load (unloading). The system dynamics are governed by a diffusion equation where the diffusion coefficient depends on stiffness. Within tendon parameter ranges, the FIB model is softer than the NH model, and so approaches steady state more slowly during loading. The presence of stiff, crimped fibrils increases bulk extension without excessively straining the fibrils, providing a natural protection mechanism for the tendon's structural components to load, in agreement with experiments. During unloading, the FIB model is much slower to relax as the tissue softens due to fibril re-crimping. This asymmetry in loading and unloading manifests as a hysteresis loop in the stress-strain curve averaged over the tendon. The hysteresis is reduced with increasing applied load. To the authors' knowledge, the finding of hysteresis within this framework is novel. The inclusion of fibrils allows for clearer biological interpretation and potential comparison to data. While the stress law employed in this study is bespoke for the application at hand by accounting for crimp and fibril recruitment, other fibril constitutive laws can readily be considered and incorporated into this framework.
item.dc:creator: Zoe C. Godard, Sarah L. Waters, Derek E. Moulton

item.title: Equivariant learning of a transferable three-dimensional classical density functional
item.description: arXiv:2608.13506v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Liquids exhibit collective behavior that depends sensitively on thermodynamic conditions, interfaces and confinement, yet predicting each new state commonly requires a separate atomistic simulation. Classical density functional theory offers a reusable variational description, but its central excess free-energy functional is generally unknown, and learned approximations for fluids have largely been developed in reduced-dimensional geometries. Here we show that this functional can be learned directly from fully three-dimensional canonical equilibrium density fields while preserving spatial symmetry and variational consistency, without free-energy or chemical-potential training labels. A functional learned from coarse three-dimensional density fields remains predictive at finer resolution, separating the sampling demands of training from the spatial resolution of subsequent predictions. A single learned functional transfers across temperatures, system sizes and statistical ensembles, and recovers the equation of state, liquid--vapor coexistence and interfacial broadening, none of which are used as training targets. Applied to complex three-dimensional geometries, it predicts the potential of mean force between colloids due to solvent mediation, and adsorption isotherms in an interconnected gyroid pore. These results demonstrate that molecular dynamics equilibrium density data can be converted into a transferable thermodynamic generator connecting microscopic liquid structure to response, phase behavior and collective phenomena.
item.dc:creator: Bingqing Cheng

item.title: Geometric Propulsion of a Scallop with Control-Dependent Hydrodynamics
item.description: arXiv:2608.24158v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study a force-free single-hinge swimmer driven by two controls. When its axial hydrodynamic connection depends only on the opening angle, we show that the mean displacement per cycle vanishes in the periodic state at any driving rate. An independent control of the hydrodynamic response removes this restriction. For a factorized connection, the displacement at arbitrary driving rate is an integral of a measurable shape moment against the hydrodynamic modulation; in the slow-driving limit it reduces to a curvature flux which, at fixed potential and connection, is independent of the shape mobility. A reflecting harmonic model illustrates how thermal fluctuations modify this flux without generating it, and a hinged-bead model with variable passive slip gives a quantitative opening--closing test of the mechanism. We distinguish these propulsion results from the leading shape-sector dissipation, which depends on the mobility and is governed by a thermodynamic metric.
item.dc:creator: Hisao Hayakawa

item.title: CBTV: Colour Bean Tracking Velocimetry for Dense Granular Flows
item.description: arXiv:2610.31883v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In a dense granular flow, a particle that moves more than about half the spacing between frames is easily confused with a neighbour, and so dense flows are recorded at high frame rates. We present Colour Bean Tracking Velocimetry (CBTV) for particles of a few distinct colours. CBTV first matches small groups of neighbours by position and colour. It then links the remaining particles by relaxation particle tracking velocimetry (PTV) among particles of the same colour, with a search radius set in each frame from the detections. CBTV was compared with ten published trackers on 15 simulated granular flows, with every tracker given the same detections and one global setting. At 2.8 to 13 diameters per frame, on four flows, CBTV keeps 0.595 of the links, against 0.338 for the best published tracker on each cell. It leads that tracker on every cell outside a rotating drum, where every method fails, and trails on none. CBTV was configured on these four flows with their ground truth in view. At steps 1 to 8, on 45 benchmark cases not used in its tuning, CBTV leads the best published tracker on 14 cases and ties on 31, with no deficit. This test is not fully out of sample, because one setting was fixed after a look at part of the benchmark. The ties lie at small displacements. On two unseen flows, a colour-gated relaxation variant built in this work kept more links than CBTV on average. All tests are simulated.
item.dc:creator: Kaveeshan Thurairajah, Zhao Pan

item.title: Lie-Poisson Formulation of Dissipative Spin Hydrodynamics
item.description: arXiv:2611.22615v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Covariance and the second law cannot fix how fluid flow couples to spin, since reversible couplings produce no entropy. We show that the spin commutation relations and the Poincar\'e algebra fix these couplings. Reversibly, a flow exerts no torque on the spin: its magnitude per particle is conserved, its direction is Fermi--Walker transported, and spin--shear couplings reflect a deforming triad. The magnitude changes only through higher multipoles, as in spinor condensates, or dissipation, whose first-order spin--shear coupling reorients the spin away from the vorticity above a critical shear rate.
item.dc:creator: Zi-Hao Liu, Mei Huang
